title: Bananas are radioactive
body: Bananas are rich in potassium, and a tiny share of all potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40. One banana delivers about 0.1 microsieverts. A chest X-ray is roughly a thousand bananas.
takeaway: Radiation is a matter of dose. Your body holds its potassium level steady, so bananas never add up.
source: US Environmental Protection Agency; Health Physics Society
visual: a single banana glowing softly on a dark laboratory bench with faint rings of energy radiating outward

title: You carry about as many bacteria as human cells
body: The old claim was ten bacteria for every human cell. A careful recount found roughly 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells in a typical adult. All those microbes together weigh only about 200 grams.
takeaway: Famous numbers get repeated for decades without being checked. This one fell in 2016.
visual: a human silhouette made of two interwoven swarms of tiny glowing particles in different colours

title: Ice floats, and that is why lakes have fish
body: Water is at its densest at 4 degrees Celsius, not at freezing. Colder water rises, so lakes freeze from the top down, and the ice insulates the liquid water underneath.
takeaway: If ice sank like most solids, lakes would freeze solid from the bottom and kill what lives in them.
source: Standard physical chemistry; US Geological Survey Water Science School
visual: a cross-section of a frozen lake in winter with fish swimming calmly in dark water beneath a pale sheet of ice

title: Each of your cells holds two metres of DNA
body: Uncoiled and laid end to end, the DNA in a single human cell would stretch about two metres. It is packed into a nucleus around six thousandths of a millimetre across by winding it around proteins called histones.
takeaway: It is like fitting 40 km of fine thread inside a tennis ball.
source: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell
visual: a luminous double helix unspooling from a tiny glowing sphere and looping far off into the darkness

title: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood
body: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one sends it around the body. The blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper rather than iron. About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, not its head.
takeaway: Intelligence evolved more than once, and it does not have to look like ours.
source: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
visual: an octopus drifting in deep blue water with its arms curling in different directions, each seemingly acting on its own

title: Old windows are thicker at the bottom, but the glass never flowed
body: Many old window panes are thicker at the bottom, and a popular story says glass is a slow liquid that has sagged over the centuries. It has not. Medieval panes were spun into uneven discs and usually fitted thick edge down. Glass at room temperature would need far longer than the age of the universe to sag.
takeaway: Glass is a solid whose atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, which helped the myth along. A neat story can stay wrong for generations.
source: Edgar Zanotto, American Journal of Physics (1998)
visual: a medieval stained-glass window with wavy uneven panes catching warm light in a stone wall

title: Tardigrades survived open space
body: In 2007, tiny eight-legged tardigrades rode outside a satellite for ten days, exposed to vacuum and radiation. Many revived and later laid healthy eggs. They survive by drying out into a dormant ball called a tun.
takeaway: Life can pause itself. Biologists study tardigrades to learn how to preserve cells and vaccines.
visual: a plump microscopic tardigrade floating serenely against the curve of the Earth and a field of stars

title: Your brain runs on about 20 watts
body: The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons. It is about 2% of body weight but uses around 20% of the body's energy at rest, about the power of a dim light bulb.
takeaway: The most capable thinking machine we know runs on less power than a laptop charger.
visual: a brain rendered as a dense web of fine glowing filaments powered by a single small old-fashioned light bulb

title: Lightning is five times hotter than the Sun's surface
body: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius. The Sun's surface is about 5,500. Thunder is that air expanding explosively. Around 44 flashes happen somewhere on Earth every second.
takeaway: Count the seconds between flash and thunder and divide by three for the distance in kilometres.
visual: a single enormous branching lightning bolt splitting a dark storm sky above a silhouetted landscape

title: A tree is built mostly from air
body: In the 1600s Jan van Helmont grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for five years. The tree gained about 74 kg. The soil lost about 57 grams. Most of a tree's dry mass is carbon taken from carbon dioxide in the air.
takeaway: Wood is captured air and water, assembled with sunlight.
source: J. B. van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae (1648)
visual: a large tree whose trunk and branches dissolve at the edges into swirling streams of air being drawn inward
